pathophysiology.summary: Anaphylaxis is a serious, rapid-onset systemic hypersensitivity reaction that compromises the airway, breathing and/or circulation. Mast cell and basophil mediators cause airway oedema, bronchospasm, vasodilation, capillary leak and sometimes myocardial depression.
keyMechanisms: Airway and breathing: tissue oedema and smooth-muscle contraction cause laryngeal swelling, bronchospasm and wheeze (commonest in food-induced anaphylaxis).

Circulation: vasodilation plus capillary leak causes distributive and hypovolaemic shock; up to 35% of blood volume can leak out within 10 minutes. Myocardial depression and ischaemic ECG changes can occur even with normal coronaries.
Posture: sitting or standing a hypotensive patient reduces venous return and has caused cardiovascular collapse and death; keep them supine (or semi-recumbent if breathless).

Why adrenaline works: alpha effects reverse vasodilation and oedema; beta effects open the airways, increase myocardial contraction and suppress mast-cell mediator release. Delay is linked to protracted and fatal reactions.
Biphasic reactions (about 5%): symptoms recur hours later without re-exposure; median time about 12 h.

symptoms: Sudden onset over minutes after a trigger (drug, food, insect sting, contrast, vaccine). Parenteral triggers act fastest.
Breathing difficulty, throat tightness, hoarseness; dizziness or collapse.
Abdominal cramps, vomiting, incontinence; anxiety or 'sense of impending doom'.
Skin and mucosal changes (flushing, urticaria, angioedema) in over 80%, but absent in up to 20%.
physicalSigns: Airway: lip, tongue or throat swelling, hoarseness, stridor.
Breathing: tachypnoea, wheeze, fatigue, cyanosis, SpO2 below 92%, confusion.
Circulation: pale, clammy, hypotension, tachycardia (bradycardia is a late, pre-arrest sign), drowsiness or coma.
redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness or tongue swelling: impending airway obstruction; most experienced person to intubate early
No improvement after two doses of IM adrenaline: refractory anaphylaxis; call critical care and start an IV adrenaline infusion
Patient on a beta-blocker with poor response: give glucagon
Never sit or stand a hypotensive patient up
precipitants: Drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, contrast, anaesthetic agents), blood products, vaccines.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Wheeze without skin, circulatory or allergen features; anaphylaxis can look identical (especially in children). If in doubt, give IM adrenaline.
Swelling of lips, tongue or airway without urticaria in a patient on an ACE inhibitor; usually does not respond to adrenaline.
Throat tightness and stridor without objective allergic features; does not respond to adrenaline.
Bradycardia, pallor, quick recovery when lying flat; no urticaria, wheeze or angioedema.
Hyperventilation, tingling; no hypotension, hypoxia, wheeze or rash. Can be hard to separate in people with previous anaphylaxis.
Skin or mucosal changes only, without airway, breathing or circulation problems: not anaphylaxis.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Sudden airway and/or breathing and/or circulation problem, usually with skin changes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Diagnosis is clinical. Treat immediately; never wait for tests.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Continuously while on adrenaline; BP at least every 5 min on an infusion
ruleIn.expectedFinding: SpO2 below 92%, hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia or ischaemic changes.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Tachycardia, tremor and pallor with normal or high BP suggest too much adrenaline: reduce the infusion.
ruleIn.normalValue: SpO2 at least 94% on air; SBP at least 90 mmHg

ruleIn.modalityTarget: 1st sample as soon as feasible (do not delay treatment); 2nd at 1–2 h (no later than 4 h) after onset; 3rd at least 24 h after resolution or at allergy clinic
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Raised (above 11.4 or 14 µg/L, or above [baseline × 1.2] + 2 µg/L).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Supports the diagnosis for the allergy clinic; results are not available acutely. A normal level does not exclude anaphylaxis (often normal in food reactions). Record exact times.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise, call for help, remove the trigger
actions: ABCDE approach; call for help (resuscitation team).
Stop the suspected drug, infusion or colloid; remove the trigger if possible.
Lie the patient flat with legs raised (semi-recumbent if breathing is difficult). Do not sit or stand them up.

clinicalManagement.title: IM adrenaline first
actions: Adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1:1000) IM into the anterolateral mid-thigh: RCUK 0.5 mg (0.5 mL) for adults and children over 12; MOH 0.3–0.5 mg.
Repeat after 5 minutes if airway, breathing or circulation problems persist (MOH: every 5–15 min as needed).
Do not give IV bolus adrenaline outside cardiac arrest or specialist hands.
Immediate intubation by the most experienced available operator.

clinicalManagement.title: Oxygen and fluids
actions: High-flow oxygen (MOH: 8–10 L/min by face mask, up to 100%).
Hypotension or poor response: rapid IV crystalloid bolus 500–1000 mL (RCUK) or 1–2 L 0.9% saline (MOH); repeat as needed. Severe shock may need 3–5 L.
Use IO access if IV access is delayed.

clinicalManagement.title: Persistent bronchospasm
actions: Salbutamol 2.5–5 mg nebulised in 3 mL saline (MOH), or 2–3 puffs MDI; repeat as needed.

clinicalManagement.title: Refractory anaphylaxis
clinicalManagement.timeframe: No improvement after two IM doses
actions: Call critical care early; keep giving IM adrenaline every 5 min until the infusion runs.

Start low-dose IV adrenaline infusion: RCUK 1 mg in 100 mL 0.9% NaCl at 0.5 mL/kg/h (about 0.1 microgram/kg/min) via a dedicated line; 1 mL/kg/h if hypotensive or hypoxic. MOH: start at 0.1 microgram/kg/min and titrate.
Continuous ECG, SpO2 and BP at least every 5 min. Titrate to the lowest effective rate.
Wean: halve as symptoms improve; 1 h after full resolution, reduce over 30 min and stop.
If still refractory: noradrenaline (or dopamine per MOH; metaraminol or vasopressin per RCUK) by expert titration.
Glucagon: MOH 1–5 mg IV over 5 min then 5–15 microgram/min infusion (rapid push causes vomiting); RCUK 1 mg IV, repeat or 1–2 mg/h. Hold the beta-blocker.
Atropine 0.5 mg IV, repeat if necessary (RCUK).

clinicalManagement.title: Adjuncts after stabilisation (never instead of adrenaline)
actions: Antihistamines are third-line and only for skin symptoms: RCUK prefers a non-sedating oral antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine). MOH lists cetirizine 10 mg IV or diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV, and famotidine 20 mg IV.
Corticosteroids: RCUK does not advise them routinely (consider hydrocortisone 200 mg IV for refractory reactions or coexisting asthma). MOH lists methylprednisolone 125 mg IV.

clinicalManagement.title: Observe and discharge safely
actions: RCUK fast-track discharge after 2 h from resolution only if: good response within 5–10 min to a single dose given within 30 min of onset, complete resolution, already has trained-in-use auto-injectors, and adequate supervision.

At least 6 h after resolution if 2 IM doses were needed or there was a previous biphasic reaction. MOH: observe 6 h if airway compromise, high adrenaline doses, coronary artery disease, asthma, or on beta-blockers or ACE inhibitors.

At least 12 h if more than 2 doses were needed, severe asthma or severe respiratory compromise, possible continuing absorption (e.g. slow-release medicines), late night presentation, or poor access to emergency care.
Before discharge: stand the patient up and check for dizziness; eat something at least 1 h before leaving. If not improving: ICU (MOH).

guidelineComparison.title: Saudi MOH protocol vs RCUK 2021

values: Cetirizine 10 mg IV or diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV; famotidine 20 mg IV
Third-line, skin only; non-sedating oral preferred; no routine H2 blocker
Not routine; consider hydrocortisone 200 mg IV in refractory reactions or asthma
1 mg/100 mL at 0.5–1 mL/kg/h (~0.1–0.2 microgram/kg/min) after 2 IM doses
Risk-stratified: 2 h, at least 6 h, or at least 12 h

guidelineComparison.note: Both agree that IM adrenaline is first-line and must never be delayed for adjuncts.

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage acute anaphylaxis in the emergency department.
pitfalls: Giving antihistamine or steroid first and delaying adrenaline.
IV bolus adrenaline outside cardiac arrest.
Missing anaphylaxis without a rash (absent in up to 20%).
Discharging early without a risk-based observation period or auto-injector.
keyPoints: If in doubt, give IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the thigh.
Repeat after 5 minutes if not better; after two doses, start an IV adrenaline infusion.
Lie the patient flat; never stand a hypotensive patient up.
Antihistamines and steroids do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems.
Tryptase at 1–2 h, refer to allergy, auto-injector on discharge.

Biphasic reaction risk and when to return.
Use of the adrenaline auto-injector (demonstrated) and an action plan.
Avoid the trigger; do not take further doses of a drug that caused anaphylaxis.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
dischargeCriteria: Complete resolution and observed for the risk-appropriate period (2, 6 or 12 h).
Adrenaline auto-injector prescribed and use demonstrated (unless drug-induced), with an action plan.
Told about biphasic reactions and to return immediately if symptoms recur.
Allergy recorded in the record; drug reactions reported to SFDA (https://ade.sfda.gov.sa).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Refer every patient to an allergist-immunologist (MOH and RCUK); take the convalescent tryptase sample there.
